data.title: ‘Watch That Cliff,’ Says Top Investor on Micron Stock
data.description:
Micron (NASDAQ:MU) has spent years being treated as a highly cyclical memory stock. Now, the AI boom has turned that old investment case on its head, creating extraordinary demand for its products and giving the company pricing power that would have been difficult to imagine not long ago. The question is whether this is a structural change or simply another peak in the memory cycle.

The latest results show just how extreme the cycle has become. Micron generated $54.2 billion in quarterly revenue, up 379% year over year, while adjusted gross margin reached a remarkable 87%. The problem for investors is that memory is notoriously cyclical, raising an obvious question: how long can those economics last?

Top investor Victor Dergunov, who ranks among the top 3% of investors on TipRanks, has been bullish on Micron during its ascent but now sees a more complicated setup.

Promotion

Curious why XOVR invested in Kalshi? Explore the long-term strategy behind the investment.

Dergunov argues that Micron could still have substantial upside over the next 12 to 18 months if AI demand remains strong. The company has just delivered another blockbuster quarter, with the huge revenue increase noted above accompanied by a rise in adjusted EPS from $3.03 to $33.42.

Importantly, the guide was just as strong. Micron called for $61.5 billion of first-quarter revenue, plus or minus $1.5 billion, compared with Wall Street expectations of roughly $57.0 billion. It forecast adjusted EPS of $38.15, plus or minus $1, versus expectations of about $35.47.

That’s all well and good, but Dergunov believes the longer-term picture is much less certain. The biggest issue is supply. As additional memory capacity comes online, particularly from Chinese manufacturers, the current shortage could eventually turn into oversupply. If that happens while AI-related demand slows, Micron could lose pricing power and see margins fall sharply.

That concern is particularly relevant because an 87% gross margin is difficult to reconcile with the economics of a cyclical hardware business. Dergunov points out that even software companies known for exceptional profitability typically operate around the 80% to 85% range. Micron expects its adjusted gross margin to dip slightly to 86.25% next quarter, but Dergunov expects a much more substantial decline once the current AI boom cools.

Near term, however, the 5-star investor sees reasons for optimism. Memory shortages remain severe, pricing is strong and earnings expectations continue to rise. Micron is expected to generate roughly $275 billion in fiscal 2027 revenue, with consensus estimates calling for around $314 billion in fiscal 2028.

The problem is the enormous range of forecasts for fiscal 2028. EPS estimates span roughly $136 to more than $335, while revenue estimates range from about $127 billion to nearly $400 billion. For Dergunov, those wide ranges highlight how little certainty there is around Micron’s earnings power once the current memory shortage fades.

Bottom line: Dergunov remains bullish on Micron in the near term, but he sees the longer-term setup as much less attractive. If new memory supply catches up with demand, particularly if AI spending cools, Micron’s pricing power and margins could come under heavy pressure.

As such, Dergunov rates MU stock a Hold. (To watch Dergunov’s track record, click here)

However, on the Street only one analyst joins Dergunov on the sidelines, while an additional 25 Buys add up to a Strong Buy consensus rating. The average price target stands at $1,581.40, implying the stock will gain 47% in the months ahead. (See Micron stock forecast)

data.title: ServiceNow vs. Microsoft: Run Away From One Software Stock, Embrace the Other, Says Investor
data.description:
Enterprise software is going through a period of reassessment as investors weigh the impact of AI on everything from employee productivity to cloud computing and software spending. Some companies might be benefiting from rising demand for AI infrastructure, but others are having to demonstrate that their existing software businesses can continue growing as customers rethink how they use technology.

That makes ServiceNow (NYSE:NOW) and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) an interesting comparison. The former remains one of the leading names in enterprise software, with strong growth despite the broader pressure on the sector, while the latter combines its enormous software business with Azure, one of the world’s largest cloud platforms.

Investor Gary Alexander has been reassessing the two companies and argues that investors need to look beyond headline growth and examine what is actually driving that growth, how much customers are committing to future spending, and whether earnings are keeping pace with valuations.

Promotion

70% Off TipRanks

  • Unlock powerful investing tools with TipRanks Premium to make smarter, more confident investment decisions
  • Subscribe to TipRanks Smart Investor Newsletter, and discover new investing opportunities with data-backed stock picks
Learn more about TipRanks Premium

ServiceNow has held up relatively well during the software sell-off, the shares falling only around 10% since the start of the year, and climbing by 65% since bottoming out in April. The company’s resilience reflects continued demand for its enterprise platform, but the rebound has also left investors paying a substantial premium for that growth.

The latest results showed revenue rising 24% year over year to $3.99 billion, beating Wall Street expectations of $3.93 billion. Subscription revenue grew 23% on a constant-currency basis, accelerating from the previous quarter, while ServiceNow slightly increased its full-year revenue guidance.

The headline numbers, however, do not tell the whole story. The company completed its $7.75 billion acquisition of cybersecurity company Armis in April, and Alexander believes the deal contributed meaningfully to the acceleration in reported subscription growth. Armis had previously disclosed annual recurring revenue of $340 million, which implies roughly $85 million of quarterly revenue when simply divided across four quarters. That would represent around three percentage points of ServiceNow’s subscription growth in the latest quarter.

The problem is that ServiceNow does not separately disclose organic and acquired growth, making it difficult to determine how much of the acceleration is coming from the underlying business. Alexander also points to remaining performance obligations, which are growing at roughly 21.5% on a constant-currency basis. That is broadly in line with revenue growth rather than running substantially ahead of it.

Profitability presents another question. ServiceNow added around 700 employees during the quarter, taking its workforce to approximately 30,500, up 12% year over year. Its adjusted operating margin consequently remained at 29.5%, giving Alexander limited evidence of the margin expansion that could help support its premium valuation.

Meanwhile, its valuation looks particularly demanding from an earnings perspective: at more than 30 times forward earnings, ServiceNow trades at roughly twice the P/E multiples of software peers such as Salesforce and Workday.

“In my view, ServiceNow’s gains are all in the rearview mirror,” Alexander summed up. “This company is becoming a souring bet as acquisitions dominate its growth story, while the company isn’t making sufficient margin progress to be able to rationalize its valuation multiples down closer to its peers.”

“Sell this stock and invest elsewhere,” the investor concluded. (To watch Alexander’s track record, click here)

Turning to Microsoft, its latest results give Alexander plenty to consider. Revenue rose 17% year over year to $90 billion, while adjusted EPS climbed 23% to $4.74. Azure was the standout, with growth accelerating to 43%, while remaining performance obligations jumped 84% to $678 billion.

The bigger question is what those numbers say about Microsoft’s enormous AI spending. So far, the company is showing that its investment in computing capacity can be monetized quickly. Microsoft says demand continues to exceed available capacity, meaning new infrastructure is being absorbed by customers rather than sitting idle while the company waits for AI demand to develop.

Alexander believes that gives Microsoft an important advantage. Azure also has the advantage of sitting on top of Microsoft’s huge existing software and cloud business, rather than having to build a new revenue stream from scratch. Microsoft can therefore use its established businesses to support its AI investments while Azure provides an important source of growth.

There are still risks to mull over. AI safety concerns could slow development, Microsoft’s exposure to OpenAI creates additional uncertainty, and AI-driven workforce reductions could eventually affect demand for software subscriptions. Commercial bookings have also been uneven. But with Azure growth accelerating and demand still exceeding capacity, Alexander sees evidence that Microsoft’s AI investments are beginning to translate into a more powerful growth engine.

Lastly, the valuation is also worth considering. Microsoft trades at roughly 26 times forward earnings, compared with more than 30 times for ServiceNow. “I continue to see more tailwinds than headwinds for Microsoft as Azure growth takes off,” the investor summed up. “Stay long here: a mid-20s P/E multiple still leaves plenty of room for upside when accelerating growth is expected ahead.”

Accordingly, Alexander rates MSFT a Buy.

Turning now to the Street’s view, we find that both are popular choices boasting Strong Buy consensus ratings. NOW’s average price target lands at $143.41, offering 12-month returns of a modest 6%. MSFT’s $575.91 average target points to one-year gains of 12%. (See NOW stock forecast or MSFT stock forecast)

data.title: ‘The Problem Is Not a Problem,’ Says Top Investor About Oracle Stock
data.description:
Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) has aggressively positioned itself right at the heart of the AI infrastructure boom, building enormous data centers to satisfy the computing demands of companies such as OpenAI.

The opportunity is enormous, but then so is the logistical challenge. Oracle needs to build facilities, secure power and bring thousands of AI chips online fast enough to turn its huge pipeline of signed contracts into revenue.

That has made Oracle’s data-center expansion one of the most closely watched stories on Wall Street. And now, a problem at its New Mexico campus has put the spotlight on whether the company can actually deliver all that promised capacity on schedule.

Promotion

200% short exposure to ORCL with ORCZ

However, investor Rick Orford, who ranks among the top 2% of investors on TipRanks, argues that investors might be concentrating too heavily on that particular project while overlooking a more important point: Oracle’s customers are still showing strong demand for its AI infrastructure.

That take was reinforced by Oracle’s latest quarterly results. The company delivered 850 megawatts of AI capacity during the first quarter, roughly 85% of the amount management had previously indicated and nearly three times the previous quarter’s figure. Its flagship Abilene, Texas, campus also reached 75% capacity delivery, despite newer projects in New Mexico, Wisconsin and Michigan contributing nothing during the quarter.

Demand, meanwhile, remained very strong. Oracle’s AI infrastructure utilization reached 97.9%, meaning almost all of its available capacity was being used. Customers renewing leases on older chips were also willing to pay around 20% more, even though most of those chips were at least four years old. For the investor, that provides an early counterpoint to the argument that AI hardware rapidly loses its economic value.

Oracle’s backlog offers another reason to focus on execution rather than demand. Remaining performance obligations rose to $664 billion, with approximately $86 billion expected to convert into revenue over the following 12 months. That represents a substantial portion of Oracle’s $90 billion fiscal 2027 revenue target, suggesting that the bigger question is whether the company can bring the required capacity online on schedule.

Customer prepayments are also helping fund the expansion. Oracle received $11.4 billion in prepayments during the quarter, equivalent to around 40% of its capital spending. That helped reduce the company’s quarterly free-cash-flow deficit considerably.

Meanwhile, Orford sees Texas as an important source of Oracle’s next wave of capacity. Vantage Data Centers is developing a 1.4-gigawatt campus in Shackelford County for Oracle and OpenAI, with its first building targeted for the second half of 2026. If that timetable holds, the site could begin adding capacity as the Abilene campus approaches completion.

New Mexico is considerably less straightforward. Project Jupiter, a 2.45-gigawatt campus for OpenAI, still depends on a gas pipeline and an on-site Bloom Energy power plant. A required air permit remains unresolved, while the pipeline’s expected start date has already slipped.

That uncertainty helps explain Oracle’s recent force majeure notice to Stack Infrastructure, the company developing Jupiter. The notice could allow Oracle to defer certain rental payments if qualifying delays prevent the project from opening as planned. Oracle has described such notices as commonplace and maintains that Jupiter remains on schedule.

Orford believes Oracle’s main problem is not a lack of demand, but the timing of when that demand turns into revenue. In his view, the market is assuming more prolonged problems than Oracle’s substantial backlog of signed contracts appears to justify. “Sure, Jupiter could easily slip further, and if a permit denial ever lines up with a stall in Texas, I’d have to revisit that view,” the 5-star investor summed up. “But until then, the Oct. 28 Investor Day and the Dec. 14 report should give us a clearer read on both campuses, and with the Texas capacity already under contract, my Buy rating for Oracle remains in place.” (To watch Orford’s track record, click here)

It’s mostly Buys among the Street’s analysts too. Based on 27 Buys vs. 4 Holds and 1 Sell, the stock receives a Strong Buy consensus rating. Going by the $245.75 average price target, a year from now shares will be changing hands for a 78% premium. (See ORCL stock forecast)

data.title: ‘Planning the Escape Route,’ Says Investor About Sandisk Stock
data.description:
The AI boom has transformed the memory market, but Sandisk’s (NASDAQ:SNDK) opportunity might have less to do with chasing AI demand than with escaping the most cyclical parts of the NAND business. The company has been rapidly shifting its mix toward data centers, where customers are signing longer-term agreements and providing greater visibility on future revenue.

That shift is notable because Sandisk’s strongest pricing in 2026 came from a part of the market that could prove difficult to defend. Edge and consumer products, including smartphones and PCs, still account for a large share of the company’s business, but their recent pricing strength was largely driven by a supply squeeze rather than underlying demand.

Investor Dustin Quasney argues that this distinction is crucial. At Citi’s Global TMT conference, Sandisk CFO Luis Visoso acknowledged that the company had been late to the data-center market and remained underrepresented there. Sandisk has since accelerated its transition, with data centers accounting for 38% of bits in the latest quarter, compared with roughly 12% a year earlier.

Promotion

Two ETFs for long or short leverage on SNDK

Quasney’s argument is that this should be viewed primarily as a defensive move. During the AI-driven NAND shortage, suppliers redirected capacity toward enterprise storage, leaving phone and PC manufacturers competing for less supply. That pushed Edge pricing sharply higher. But as additional NAND capacity arrives, Quasney expects that advantage to unwind, particularly because smartphone and PC demand remains under pressure.

The contrast with data centers is important. Sandisk’s newer business models are backed by multi-year commitments, financial guarantees and pricing floors. Management expects these arrangements to cover more than half of its bits in FY27 and roughly two-thirds in FY28. Quasney therefore expects the proportion of Sandisk’s business exposed to quarter-to-quarter market pricing to fall substantially over the next 18 months.

That could change how investors should think about the company. Sandisk may still operate in a cyclical industry, but a much larger portion of its output could soon be protected by contracts while its data-center exposure continues to expand. Quasney estimates that data-center bits could represent roughly 50% to 56% of total output by late 2027.

The main risk is timing. If Edge pricing collapses before Sandisk has completed its transition, the company could still experience a significant earnings hit. There are also longer-term concerns around new NAND capacity, competition in enterprise storage and whether data-center demand itself eventually becomes cyclical.

For Quasney, however, the market is still valuing Sandisk largely as a conventional memory-cycle stock. The central thesis is that its business is changing faster than that valuation suggests: less exposure to spot pricing, more contracted revenue and a much greater presence in data centers.

To this end, Quasney rates SNDK stock a Buy. (To watch Quasney’s track record, click here)

So do most of the Street’s analysts. The stock’s Strong Buy consensus rating is based on 15 Buys and 2 Holds. Shares are expected to gain 25% over the coming months, given the average price target clocks in at $2,195.29. (See SNDK stock forecast)

data.title: Broadcom vs. Marvell: One AI Stock Offers More Bang for the Buck, Says Top Investor
data.description:
Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO) and Marvell (NASDAQ:MRVL) are two prominent chipmakers that have been delivering strong results as AI spending continues to reshape the semiconductor industry.

Broadcom’s AI semiconductor revenue is growing at an extraordinary rate, while Marvell is seeing rapid expansion in its data-center business as demand rises for custom silicon, connectivity and memory infrastructure. Both companies are also deepening their relationships with major hyperscalers, giving them exposure to some of the biggest AI infrastructure projects.

Yet there remains a significant gap in scale. Broadcom is a semiconductor giant, and while Marvell is no minnow, it is smaller and vying to capture a bigger piece of the AI pie.

Promotion

70% Off TipRanks

  • Unlock powerful investing tools with TipRanks Premium to make smarter, more confident investment decisions
  • Subscribe to TipRanks Smart Investor Newsletter, and discover new investing opportunities with data-backed stock picks
Learn more about TipRanks Premium

Does that mean Marvell offers a better opportunity for investors given it has more room to grow? Not necessarily, says an investor using the pseudonym Bay Area Ideas (BAI), who ranks among the top 4% of investors on TipRanks.

Looking at Broadcom, BAI notes that its latest quarter was difficult to ignore. Fiscal Q3 revenue climbed 86% year over year to $29.59 billion, accelerating dramatically from 48% growth in Q2 and marking the fifth consecutive quarter of accelerating growth. AI semiconductor revenue was even stronger, soaring 221% to $16.7 billion. Management expects another acceleration in Q4, with AI semiconductor revenue forecast to rise 236%.

The outlook goes well beyond the next quarter. Broadcom now expects $58 billion in AI revenue for FY2026, followed by $115 billion in FY2027 and $230 billion in FY2028. In other words, management is projecting that AI revenue could quadruple over two years. BAI sees this as evidence that the current AI infrastructure boom is not simply a short-term surge.

The company’s profitability has also remained solid despite the changing revenue mix. Gross margin fell from 78% a year earlier to 75% as semiconductors made up a larger share of sales, but operating margin increased to 68%. Adjusted EPS rose 96% year over year, suggesting that Broadcom is still converting its rapid revenue growth into substantial earnings growth.

BAI also sees another piece of the story in VMware. Broadcom has been adding products focused on private AI clouds, security and managing AI agents, giving its software operation a potential role in the next phase of enterprise AI adoption.

That’s not to say there aren’t risks involved here. Tariffs could affect Broadcom’s supply chain, while its decision to lend Anthropic up to $42 billion has raised questions about circular financing within the AI ecosystem. If AI infrastructure spending were to slow materially, arrangements like this could create additional financial risk.

Even so, BAI points to Broadcom’s valuation as an important counterweight. Its forward P/E has fallen to around 30, despite the acceleration in its business. The investor also notes that its forward PEG ratio is substantially below the IT sector median, meaning the valuation has not risen in line with the company’s growth expectations.

Put all that together and BAI rates AVGO stock a Buy. (To watch Bay Area Idea’s track record, click here)

Marvell’s latest results were also strong, although the numbers tell a somewhat different story. Fiscal Q2 revenue increased 37% year over year to $2.74 billion, while data-center revenue grew 46%. That marked the second consecutive quarter of accelerating growth and confirmed that demand for AI-related infrastructure is translating into higher sales.

Marvell has several avenues for further expansion. Its CXL memory products target the growing requirements of AI systems, while its optical technology addresses the need for greater bandwidth inside data centers. The company is also deepening its relationships with hyperscalers, including Google, and could benefit from custom-chip programs involving other major cloud companies.

Q3 guidance points to another sharp acceleration, with revenue expected to reach approximately $3.15 billion, representing 52% year-over-year growth. The complication is profitability. Gross-margin pressure is expected to persist as the faster-growing custom business carries lower margins, creating a headwind as its contribution to revenue increases, while projected adjusted EPS growth is below the anticipated rate of revenue growth.

Nevertheless, BAI sees Marvell’s investment in India as a longer-term opportunity, particularly as the country’s semiconductor and AI ecosystem develops. However, the investor’s main concern remains the valuation. Marvell’s forward P/E is around 63, far above both its historical average and the broader IT sector.

So, while Marvell has an impressive growth pipeline and strong hyperscaler exposure, its valuation leaves less room for execution issues or further margin weakness.

To this end, BAI rates MRVL stock a Hold (i.e., Neutral).

The word on the Street is that both these stocks are Strong Buys. AVGO is expected to appreciate by 51% over the next year, given its average price target lands at $519.21. Based on an average target of $268.08, MRVL should notch returns of 12%. (See AVGO stock forecast or MRVL stock forecast)

data.title: Palantir vs. SK hynix: One AI Stock Is a Long-Term Opportunity, the Other Is Bound to Disappoint, Says Top Investor
data.description:
Palantir (NASDAQ:PLTR) and SK hynix (NASDAQ:SKHY) have both benefited from the AI boom, but their businesses operate at different ends of the technology supply chain.

Palantir helps companies turn their data into something useful through AI-powered software, while South Korea-based SK hynix supplies the memory chips needed to keep AI systems running. Both companies have enjoyed extraordinary growth, although their future prospects depend on very different factors.

Palantir has reached a market cap of around $450 billion, supported by surging revenue, strong margins, and growing demand for its software. However, the valuation is demanding, with shares trading at approximately 56 times expected 2026 revenue and around 100 times guided adjusted free cash flow. SK hynix, meanwhile, has approached a $1 trillion valuation as a shortage of DRAM and NAND memory has sent prices soaring.

Promotion

Curious why XOVR invested in Kalshi? Explore the long-term strategy behind the investment.

But moving forward from here, a 5-star investor with the nom de plume of The Value Portfolio (TVP) sees a fundamental difference between the two: Palantir’s growth could prove more durable, while SK hynix faces the risk that today’s exceptional profitability will attract too much competition and production capacity.

Looking at Palantir, TVP takes a bullish stance, pointing to its ability to help businesses implement AI rather than simply experiment with it. The company’s latest results highlight that opportunity. US revenue grew 115% year over year, while US commercial revenue climbed 149%. Customer numbers increased 35%, and the company secured more than $2 billion in total contract value during the quarter, up 153% from a year earlier.

The scale of these deals matters because Palantir can spread its development costs across a growing customer base while maintaining substantial margins. Its annualized free cash flow is approaching $5 billion, with a margin of approximately 63%. Management’s full-year revenue guidance exceeds $8.15 billion, while adjusted free cash flow is expected to reach $4.6 billion.

TVP argues that businesses still struggle to deploy AI effectively, creating an opportunity for Palantir’s software to become an important part of their operations. The company has spent years developing its platform and can finance further development internally. Although its current free cash flow yield is only around 1%, TVP believes continued rapid growth could eventually make the valuation more reasonable.

The main concern is competition from well-funded AI companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic, as well as the possibility that Palantir’s growth fails to justify its lofty valuation. Nevertheless, TVP sees Palantir as a “valuable long-term investment opportunity,” despite its expensive valuation.

To this end, TVP rates PLTR stock as a Buy. (To watch The Value Portfolio’s track record, click here)

SK hynix presents a different investment case. Its recent profitability has been extraordinary, with operating profit surging more than 550% year over year as DRAM and NAND prices climbed sharply. The company has also strengthened its balance sheet, building a substantial net cash position.

However, TVP warns that today’s high profit margins may not last. Memory manufacturing is cyclical, and high prices encourage manufacturers to expand production. SK hynix plans to triple its wafer capacity by 2034, while South Korea, China, and the United States are supporting substantial investments in domestic semiconductor manufacturing.

That expansion could eventually create an oversupply if production grows faster than demand. Competition from China’s CXMT is another concern, with the company gaining market share rapidly. Meanwhile, high memory prices are putting pressure on customers’ budgets, raising questions about how much additional demand the market can sustain.

TVP estimates that SK hynix could triple production while eventually returning to its pre-boom profit margins. Under that scenario, the investor calculates that the stock could be worth around $48 per ADR by 2035, substantially below current levels. Ultimately, TVP views SK hynix as vulnerable to a supply glut and declining margins. “I see SKHY as a poor long-term investment, unlikely to match S&P 500 growth, unless AI demand remains exceptionally strong,” TVP, who ranks among the top 5% of investors on TipRanks, summed up.

As such, TVP rates SKHY a Sell.

On the Street, PLTR claims a Moderate Buy consensus rating, while its $201 average price target offers one-year upside of 6%. SKHY draws a more favorable outlook; it is rated a Strong Buy, with its $254.70 average target pointing to 12-month returns of 32%. (See PLTR stock forecast or SKHY stock forecast)

data.title: ‘Don’t Miss This,’ Says Citi About Rocket Lab Stock
data.description:
Rocket Lab (NASDAQ:RKLB) stock is ticking higher in Thursday’s session as investors digest a major new commercial launch agreement. The company has signed its largest-ever commercial Electron contract with Japanese Earth-imaging company Synspective, covering 20 launches between 2028 and 2031. The deal takes Synspective’s total contracted Electron missions to 47 and pushes Rocket Lab’s overall launch backlog above 100 missions.

Separately, a new note from Citi analyst John Godyn has laid out a strong bull case for the space company. Godyn sees Rocket Lab as much more than a rocket manufacturer and has outlined several reasons why the company could benefit from the expansion of the space economy, ranging from demand for its existing launch services to its plans for a larger rocket and its proposed acquisition of Iridium Communications.

First of all, Godyn believes Wall Street is underestimating demand for launches. Satellite networks are expanding, with governments and commercial operators looking to put more equipment into low Earth orbit. These networks need reliable access to space, and the analyst expects demand for launch capacity to exceed current expectations.

Promotion

70% Off TipRanks

  • Unlock powerful investing tools with TipRanks Premium to make smarter, more confident investment decisions
  • Subscribe to TipRanks Smart Investor Newsletter, and discover new investing opportunities with data-backed stock picks
Learn more about TipRanks Premium

Rocket Lab has several ways to benefit from that demand. Its Electron rocket is already carrying satellites into orbit, but the company also manufactures spacecraft, components and optical systems, while providing services to customers operating satellites in space.

Godyn also sees plenty of room for Electron to grow. The rocket has already deployed more than 200 spacecraft for commercial and government customers, including NASA and U.S. defense agencies. As satellite operators expand their networks, Rocket Lab could secure more launches without having to rely on a new vehicle to drive the business forward.

Then there is Neutron. The larger, reusable rocket is designed to carry payloads of up to 13,000 kilograms, opening the door to bigger satellite constellations and national security missions. Godyn expects its first flight in the first quarter of 2027, followed by a ramp-up in launches over the next two years. The analyst sees Neutron as a major step forward, although its commercial success will depend on execution and demand.

Additionally, Rocket Lab’s planned acquisition of Iridium could take the company beyond launch services and satellite manufacturing. Announced at a value of roughly $8 billion, the deal would add Iridium’s global satellite communications network and spectrum to Rocket Lab’s existing operations. Godyn sees this as a way to participate directly in the services built around space infrastructure.

Furthermore, the analyst points to Rocket Lab’s combination of technologies, manufacturing capabilities and launch facilities. Having several parts of the process under one roof could help the company develop systems faster and serve customers across different markets.

Finally, Godyn argues that Rocket Lab owns assets that would be difficult for competitors to reproduce. As demand for space-based services grows, the investor believes these capabilities could help Rocket Lab defend its position and capture more of the market.

“As one of the only companies on the planet delivering regular commercial access to orbit, we believe RKLB’s proven launch vehicle (Electron), deep portfolio of space technology, launch infrastructure and vertically integrated growth flywheel uniquely positions the company within the space industry landscape,” Godyn summed up. “We see RKLB as an industry leader in developing and monetizing all of the opportunities – be it launch, spacecraft/technology, or applications – that are being created by the rapid expansion of the space economy. In other words, we believe RKLB is a core holding for space bulls.”

To this end, Godyn initiated coverage of RKLB stock with a Buy rating, backed by a $105 price target. Should the figure be met, investors will be pocketing returns of 45% a year from now. (To watch Godyn’s track record, click here)

The Street’s average target is actually a little higher. At $110.07, the figure makes room for one-year gains of 57%. All told, based on 12 Buys vs. 2 Holds, the analyst consensus rates the stock a Strong Buy. (See RKLB stock forecast)

data.title: ‘There’s a Reason,’ Says Investor About Oracle Stock
data.description:
For Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) investors, the past year has been a miserable one,with shares down more than 50% from last October’s highs. The decline reflects concerns about Oracle’s transformation from a traditional software provider into a major AI infrastructure and data-center player, bringing with it a much larger capital burden and significantly more financial risk.

The biggest concern is that Oracle is now spending enormous amounts of money upfront in anticipation of future AI-related revenue. That spending has pushed the company toward external financing, while a substantial portion of the expected revenue is tied to OpenAI.

Investor Prakhar Agarwal argues that while the backlog is substantial, it is not the same as realized revenue, particularly when so much of it depends on a single customer.

Promotion

ORCZ: built for a short position on ORCL

At the same time, Oracle’s current financial position deserves particular scrutiny. The company spent roughly $28.5 billion on capital expenditures in its latest quarter, exceeding its $23.1 billion in operating cash flow. Net debt has climbed above $169 billion, while debt and debt-like obligations are substantially higher when leases and purchase commitments are included. Oracle also has around $288 billion of additional lease commitments and approximately $34 billion in unconditional purchase commitments.

That financing burden becomes more important if AI spending slows. Unlike some of its larger hyperscaler peers, Oracle has less balance-sheet flexibility to absorb a prolonged period of heavy investment without relying on debt or equity markets. It has already completed a $20 billion at-the-market equity offering and raised another roughly $5 billion through mandatory convertible preferred shares, highlighting its need for outside capital.

Agarwal also questions how much of the enormous AI infrastructure spending should actually be considered growth. Higher chip, memory and other component prices mean hyperscalers are paying considerably more for the same underlying equipment. Oracle therefore faces not only the risk of spending heavily on new capacity, but also the risk that the cost of building that capacity remains elevated.

The debt market is already reflecting some of these concerns. Oracle’s credit-default-swap spreads have risen sharply, while a long-dated bond has recently yielded above 8%. Its BBB rating from S&P also leaves relatively little room before investment-grade status becomes a more significant concern.

So, although the valuation has fallen substantially, Agarwal argues that this does not automatically make the stock cheap. With leverage high, capital requirements substantial, customer concentration significant and future AI returns still uncertain, investors should take a cautious stance. “The margin of safety remains low, while execution risk still remains material,” the investor summed up.

For those reasons, Agarwal maintains a Hold (i.e., Neutral) rating on Oracle. (To watch Agarwal’s track record, click here)

Some Street analysts agree with that stance, but the majority have a more upbeat take. With a mix of 27 Buys, 4 Holds and 1 Sell, the stock claims a Strong Buy consensus rating. The forecast calls for 12-month returns of 79%, given the average price target stands at $245.75. (See ORCL stock forecast)

data.title: ‘This Changes the Story,’ Says Top Investor About AMD Stock
data.description:
AMD (NASDAQ:AMD) has had a huge run over the past year as investors have piled into the chipmaker’s growing role in artificial intelligence. The company has been gaining ground in both GPUs and CPUs, while major deals with companies such as OpenAI have strengthened its position in the AI infrastructure market.

Now, AMD is making another major move that could broaden its AI ambitions beyond traditional computing. The company recently agreed to acquire World Labs, the spatial intelligence startup founded by AI researcher Fei-Fei Li, in an $8.2 billion all-stock deal.

Foord had previously been cautious about AMD, pointing to concerns over margins and execution even as the broader AI opportunity remained compelling. Those concerns have since eased. That gives AMD exposure to what Foord believes could be the next major phase of AI: physical AI. The OpenAI warrants also remain a potential source of dilution, with OpenAI able to receive up to 160 million AMD shares if the agreement’s milestones are met.

Still, Foord believes the investment case has changed. AMD is no longer simply competing for a larger share of the existing AI chip market. With World Labs, the company is positioning itself for an AI ecosystem that could eventually extend from computers into the physical world, potentially creating another source of demand for its GPUs and CPUs.

data.title: Why Accenture Stock Is Surging Today, and Why This Analyst Says the Reaction Is “Overly Optimistic”
data.description:
Accenture (NYSE:ACN) investors are having a day to remember. Shares are up by more than 18% in Thursday’s session after the consulting and technology-services giant reported fiscal fourth-quarter results that beat expectations across revenue, earnings and bookings.

Revenue came in at $18.68 billion, up 6% year over year, or 7% in local currency. That was ahead of both Accenture’s guidance of $17.75 billion to $18.40 billion and the $18.03 billion consensus estimate. Local-currency growth also accelerated sharply from 3% in the fiscal third quarter, with all three geographic regions growing 7%. Consulting and managed services both posted 7% growth as well.

Bookings were another positive, reaching $22.2 billion and growing 5% in local currency. That produced a book-to-bill ratio of 1.2, up from 1.0 in the previous quarter. The breakdown was also stronger in managed services, which posted a 1.4 book-to-bill ratio, while consulting came in at 1.0. Adjusted diluted earnings per share reached $3.29, up 8% from a year earlier and ahead of the Street’s $3.18 estimate.

  • Subscribe to TipRanks Smart Investor Newsletter, and discover new investing opportunities with data-backed stock picks

Accenture also provided its initial outlook for fiscal 2027. The company expects revenue to grow between 3% and 6% in local currency, while adjusted EPS is projected to come in between $14.39 and $14.81. The $14.60 midpoint is above the $14.64 consensus estimate, although below the analyst’s own $14.97 forecast. Accenture expects acquisitions to contribute around 2% to 2.5% of revenue growth in fiscal 2027, compared with roughly 1.5% in fiscal 2026.

So, investors evidently liked what was on offer, but William Blair analyst Maggie Nolan thinks the reaction is “overly optimistic.”

On the plus side, Nolan notes that several concerns behind her June downgrade were addressed during the quarter. Consulting growth recovered to 7% in local currency from just 1% in the previous quarter, while the health and public service business returned to growth. Bookings also recovered, with the 1.2 book-to-bill ratio marking a clear improvement from the prior quarter.

However, the analyst is more cautious about the fiscal 2027 outlook. While the 3% to 6% revenue-growth range looks solid compared with expectations, roughly 2% to 2.5% is expected to come from acquisitions. Nolan calculates that this leaves organic growth somewhere between roughly 0.5% and 4%, with about 2% at the midpoint.

That would be below the roughly 3% organic growth Accenture generated in fiscal 2026. For Nolan, the strong fourth quarter therefore needs to be viewed alongside the possibility that the underlying business could grow more slowly next year, even as acquisitions provide a larger contribution to the overall revenue figure.

The first-quarter guidance also points to a deceleration, with the 4% midpoint for local-currency growth below the fourth-quarter rate. The $14.60 midpoint of the EPS outlook is broadly in line with consensus rather than meaningfully above it. The analyst also acknowledges Accenture’s continued focus on margins and its strong cash generation. “However,” Nolan added, “the fourth-quarter organic contribution is not yet quantified, M&A activity is contributing more, and we have limited visibility into how much of the consulting rebound is organic and AI-driven. We would like more evidence that the acceleration is durable before turning more constructive.”

To this end, Nolan reiterated a Market Perform (i.e., Neutral) rating, without having a fixed price target in mind. (To watch Nolan’s track record, click here)

data.title: ‘Some Kind of Fantasy,’ Says Investor About Micron Stock
data.description:
Micron (NASDAQ:MU) just delivered the kind of earnings report that would normally send a stock flying, yet the initial market reaction has been notably muted, with the shares subsequently tilting into the red despite the strong beats and estimate-trouncing outlook.

In its fiscal fourth quarter, revenue came in at $54.23 billion vs. Wall Street’s roughly $51.1 billion estimate, while adjusted EPS of $33.42 topped expectations of around $31.6. Micron also posted an adjusted gross margin of 87%, and its fiscal Q1 2027 outlook was even more striking, with revenue guided to $61.5 billion at the midpoint compared to the $57.0 billion the Street was after, while adjusted EPS of $38.15 was well above the $35.40 expected by analysts.

Yet there is a fairly obvious reason for the lack of fireworks. Micron shares have already had an enormous run, so investors are no longer impressed simply by another spectacular beat. The bigger question is whether these earnings can last. Memory is notoriously cyclical, and investors are wary of extrapolating peak pricing and margins too far into the future. The one sticking point – a slightly softer gross-margin outlook for the next quarter – also gave the market some pause for thought.

Promotion

Curious why XOVR invested in Kalshi? Explore the long-term strategy behind the investment.

However, the strength of the print is hard to deny. An investor known as Agar Capital (AC) was already bullish on Micron heading into the report, but even AC underestimated how strong the quarter would be, saying the results “don’t look real.” Revenue and earnings both came in above AC’s previous estimates, while the company’s Q1 revenue outlook exceeded even the upper end of the investor’s bullish scenario.

The more important takeaway, however, was what Micron said about the supply-demand environment. Management expects memory conditions to remain tight through 2027 and 2028, suggesting the current earnings boom may have more room to run.

AC also believes the 86.25% gross-margin forecast for Q1 needs some context. The sequential decline from 87% is partly related to higher incentive compensation costs that were incorporated into inventory during the fourth quarter and will flow through earnings when that inventory is sold. Micron expects Q1 to be the low point for fiscal 2027 margins, meaning the decline should not automatically be interpreted as deteriorating memory pricing.

Another part of the story is Micron’s Strategic Customer Agreements. The company now has 26 such agreements, up from 16, with customer financial commitments reaching $32 billion. AC sees these multiyear commitments as potentially important because they provide greater visibility into future demand and could make Micron’s earnings less volatile than in previous memory cycles. They do not eliminate cyclicality, but they could soften its impact.

AC also points beyond HBM. Micron’s data-center SSD revenue reached almost $10 billion in Q4, showing how AI infrastructure is driving demand across both memory and storage. Meanwhile, the company generated $33.2 billion of adjusted free cash flow during the quarter.

Still, AC is not ignoring the memory cycle. Prices, demand and the timing of new capacity remain the key variables, and Micron will eventually face the same capacity risks that have defined previous memory cycles. But the latest results give AC more confidence that this particular period of exceptional profitability could last considerably longer than the market has historically allowed for Micron.

The combination of tight supply, AI-driven demand, growing data-center storage sales and multiyear customer commitments has changed the picture for AC. “Compared to the preview, I see more evidence that this period of exceptional earnings could last longer than the market is accustomed to granting Micron,” the investor summed up.

Accordingly, Agar Capital maintained a Strong Buy rating on the shares. (To watch Agar Capital’s track record, click here)

The Street’s analysts agree. Based on a mix of 23 Buys vs. 1 Hold, the stock claims a Strong Buy consensus rating. Going by the $1,545 average price target, shares will be changing hands for a 47% premium a year from now. (See MU stock forecast)

data.title: Meta vs. Oracle: One AI Stock Is Overvalued, the Other Offers Opportunity, Says Investor
data.description:
Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) and Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) are both spending enormous sums to build out AI infrastructure, but the way they are funding that spending could hardly be more different.

Meta is largely using its own cash flow to finance infrastructure that supports its own products and services. Oracle, meanwhile, is building data-center capacity against customer commitments, with customers helping fund that expansion through prepayments and other financing arrangements. That distinction has become particularly important as investors focus on free cash flow, debt and the eventual payoff from AI spending.

An investor using the pseudonym The Alpha Analyst (AA) has been examining this part of the AI market and sees Meta and Oracle as two of the more interesting names within the broader group of companies shouldering the AI infrastructure bill. While the overall group has faced questions about depreciation, capital intensity and how quickly those investments will generate returns, AA argues that the two companies now offer very contrasting setups.

Promotion

METQ: built for a short position on META

For Meta, the biggest issue is that the enormous AI spending is beginning to put meaningful pressure on cash generation before the associated revenue streams have fully developed. Meta spent roughly $51 billion on capital expenditure during the first half of the year and expects full-year spending of around $130 billion to $145 billion. That leaves a substantial amount of spending still to come, potentially pushing free cash flow into negative territory during the second half.

At the same time, Meta’s core advertising business remains strong. Ad revenue grew about 27%, with both advertising impressions and prices showing healthy growth. The problem for AA is that the newer AI-related revenue streams have yet to reach a scale that justifies the expectations reflected in the stock.

Meta’s newer revenue streams are growing quickly, but they remain small relative to the company’s core advertising business. Other revenue within the Family of Apps reached $1.0 billion in Q2, up 73% year over year, driven primarily by WhatsApp paid messaging and subscriptions. That’s a meaningful growth rate, but the business still represented only around 1.7% of Meta’s total quarterly revenue. Meanwhile, Reality Labs continues to generate substantial losses, while overall expenses are rising much faster than revenue.

AA is also skeptical that the recent excitement surrounding Meta’s Muse AI assistant can immediately support the valuation investors have assigned to it. The service would need a very large paying subscriber base to generate enough earnings to justify the market-value increase associated with the recent rally.

As such, due to “overvalued AI monetization, worsening Reality Labs losses, and imminent negative FCF from heavy capex,” The Alpha Analyst rates META stock a Sell. (To watch The Alpha Analyst’s track record, click here)

Oracle’s case looks quite different once you get past the issue niggling investors. Its share-price decline has been driven heavily by concerns over debt, capital spending and negative free cash flow. Yet AA points to signs that the financing burden may be starting to improve.

In Q1 FY2027, Oracle’s remaining performance obligations (RPO) climbed to roughly $664 billion, with much of the latest growth coming from arrangements that require less incremental funding from Oracle itself. Net cash capital expenditure is now expected to remain at or below roughly $70 billion, compared with gross spending of around $90 billion to $95 billion.

Demand also remains strong. GPU utilization was close to 98%, while customers renewing older GPU capacity have reportedly accepted substantially higher prices. Oracle’s infrastructure business is translating that demand into faster operating-income growth, while its huge backlog provides considerable visibility into future revenue.

That leaves Oracle with a significant debt burden, but AA argues that the valuation already reflects much of that concern. Oracle’s forward EV/EBITDA multiple is around 10.7x, well below its five-year average. If cash spending stabilizes while demand and contracted revenue continue to hold up, there is room for the market to reassess the company’s valuation.

Accordingly, with “customer-funded capex inflecting, robust contract prepayments, and strong GPU utilization supporting a contrarian rerating opportunity,” AA rates ORCL stock a Buy.

The Street, however, likes both these names. Both receive Strong Buy consensus ratings. META’s average price target lands at $800.90, pointing to 12-month returns of 10.5%. ORCL, meanwhile, is expected to gain 79%, considering its average target clocks in at $245.75. (See META stock forecast or ORCL stock forecast)

data.title: ‘It’s Too Much,’ Says Investor About Oracle Stock
data.description:
Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) stock has had a rough ride over the past year, falling roughly 55% from its October 2025 high as investors have grown concerned about its heavy AI infrastructure spending, mounting debt and the large gap between capital expenditures and operating cash flow.

Recent reports about Oracle issuing a force majeure notice connected to the Stargate AI infrastructure project in New Mexico have added to the uncertainty. The notice relates to potential delays in completing the facility and could provide Oracle with contractual protection if the project is not delivered on time. However, the bigger issue for investors is not the notice itself, but how Oracle will finance its enormous AI infrastructure expansion.

Oracle spent about $55.7 billion on capital expenditures in fiscal 2026 while generating roughly $32 billion in operating cash flow, leaving a funding gap of almost $24 billion. That has forced the company to rely on outside financing, including debt and equity, while customer prepayments have also helped fund construction. This is a key reason Oracle trades at a much lower valuation than major hyperscalers. The market is essentially waiting to see whether the billions being spent on AI infrastructure will eventually generate enough cash to fund further growth.

Promotion

ORCZ: built for a short position on ORCL

However, looking at its current situation, investor Benjamin C. Barry believes Oracle’s valuation now provides an opportunity, with the stock trading at around 16 times expected fiscal 2027 earnings. For Barry, the potential upside depends on Oracle proving that its cloud investments can pay for themselves.

The force majeure notice should therefore be viewed mainly as a contractual safeguard rather than evidence that Oracle is abandoning the Stargate project. Barry’s bigger concern is whether the company can complete its data-center expansion without taking on excessive debt, issuing more stock or paying unnecessarily high financing costs.

Oracle’s rapidly growing cloud infrastructure business is central to the thesis. Cloud infrastructure revenue recently increased by more than 120%, while the company has continued adding data-center capacity and deploying GPUs. Barry argues that the enormous backlog, including $664 billion in RPO (remaining performance obligations), gives Oracle significant contracted demand. But backlog alone is not enough. It needs to translate into revenue and, ultimately, free cash flow.

Barry also sees Oracle’s database business as an important competitive advantage. Its software is deeply embedded in the operations of companies and institutions, making it costly and difficult for customers to replace. That gives Oracle an established route into AI workloads involving sensitive private data, inference and other cloud services, something the other hyperscalers do not have to the same extent. That established position could help Oracle capture a greater portion of AI-driven cloud spending and helps explain the company’s substantial backlog.

“Oracle, however, still needs to prove that it can generate free cash flow from that growth,” Barry summed up. “It should be trading at a discount until that happens, but the discount seems too steep at this point, and that’s why I recommend initiating a position in this stock.”

To this end, Barry rates ORCL stock a Buy. (To watch Barry’s track record, click here)

Most of the Street’s analysts take a similar stance. Based on a mix of 27 Buys, 4 Holds, and 1 Sell, the stock claims a Strong Buy consensus rating. Going by the $245.75 average price target, shares will gain 78% in the months ahead. (See Oracle stock forecast)

data.title: ‘SpaceX Stock Is a Hype Play,’ Says Investor
data.description:
SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) might only be a newly public company, but it is already one of the most valuable companies in the world, with a market cap hovering around the $2 trillion mark. That figure reflects enormous expectations for the company’s future, particularly around artificial intelligence, Starlink and its ambitions in space.  

Its latest quarter showed impressive revenue growth, but the underlying numbers suggest that much of the valuation depends on future success in AI and other ambitious projects rather than the profitability of the business today.

The company generated $7.8 billion in revenue in its first publicly reported quarter, up 66% sequentially and 92% year over year. But at its current $2 trillion market cap, that still amounts to a very demanding valuation, with annualized revenue implying a price-to-sales ratio of around 64x.

Promotion

SPCX has a long & short ETF? Explore SPCM & SPCG

Investor Gytis Zizys argues that the most important distinction is between SpaceX’s three main businesses. Connectivity, largely Starlink, generated 55% of revenue and produced $1.66 billion of operating income, giving it a 38.6% operating margin. AI revenue grew an extraordinary 247% year over year to $2.56 billion, but the segment still lost about $1.26 billion at the operating level. Space generated $962 million of revenue but lost roughly $542 million.

That leaves Starlink as the only segment making a substantial positive contribution. Zizys sees considerable potential in the business as coverage expands and services improve, but argues that the space operation itself is unlikely to transform SpaceX’s financial picture anytime soon. Successful launches might generate plenty of excitement around the stock, but they do not necessarily translate into meaningful profits.

AI is the bigger question. SpaceX spent approximately $18.4 billion on capital expenditures during the quarter, with AI accounting for much of the investment, while free cash flow was around negative $25 billion over six months. Zizys expects this spending to moderate eventually, but believes the AI business needs extraordinary revenue growth to justify the scale of investment.

The investor is also skeptical of the assumptions being used to support the valuation. Management is targeting a $100 billion annualized revenue run rate, while SpaceX’s acquisition of Cursor adds another major growth opportunity but also involves issuing substantial equity.

Zizys’ valuation model uses analyst estimates rather than the more aggressive forecasts from some Wall Street firms. Even with strong revenue growth and expanding margins, the model produces a fair value of roughly $91-$92 per share, implying substantial downside from current levels.

Essentially, Zizys’ main concern is that SpaceX has a lot of growth potential, but its $2 trillion valuation already assumes a huge amount of future success, especially in AI. The company still has to prove that it can turn that growth into sustainable profits. For Zizys, the fundamentals simply aren’t strong enough yet to support the price investors are currently paying.

A big part of that valuation, the investor argues, comes down to Elon Musk’s ability to sell the story and keep investors excited about what comes next. “At this price, SPCX is mostly a hype play and only good for traders,” Zizys summed up. “I am not looking to trade my stocks.”

Accordingly, Zizys rates SPCX stock a Strong Sell. (To watch Zizys’ track record, click here)

data.title: Joby vs. Archer: One eVTOL Stock Is Now a Buy, but the Other Lacks Clarity, Says Investor
data.description:
Joby Aviation (NYSE:JOBY) and Archer Aviation (NYSE:ACHR) are still competing to establish themselves in the emerging eVTOL market, but the investment case for the two companies has changed.

The question is no longer simply which company will get its aircraft certified first. With certification timelines still uncertain and higher interest rates making distant revenue projections less attractive, investors also need to consider which company has more ways to generate revenue while it waits.

That shift has changed the relative appeal of the two stocks. Joby still has the clearer lead on certification and has meaningful commercial activity already underway, but Archer has substantially broadened its business through its planned acquisition of three Boeing subsidiaries.

Promotion

Double your ACHR exposure with Tradr's ARCX

An investor using the moniker The Alpha Analyst (AA) previously recommended a pair trade involving Joby and Archer, taking a bullish position on Joby while using a short position in Archer to hedge the broader risks facing the eVTOL sector. At the time, AA believed Joby was better positioned because it was further ahead on certification and closer to commercial operations. Since then, however, both stocks have fallen sharply, while Archer has transformed its business through its planned acquisition of three Boeing subsidiaries. Those developments have changed the balance between the two stocks, leading AA to close the pair trade.

It’s true that Joby remains ahead when it comes to certification. It has five aircraft flying, including one that conforms to FAA standards, putting it further along the regulatory process than Archer. Joby also expects roughly $115 million to $125 million of revenue this year, while seats sold rose about 50% year over year in the second quarter. Those are meaningful signs of operational progress.

The problem is that certification remains the key variable for Joby’s valuation, and there is still no firm date for the next major step in the process. Its federal eVTOL pilot program could also compete for resources with certification work. In other words, Joby has made progress, but much of the long-term investment case still depends on clearing the regulatory hurdle.

Archer has a different story now. Its agreement to acquire Boeing’s Insitu, Wisk and SkyGrid businesses gives the company exposure beyond passenger air taxis. Insitu is particularly important because the defense drone company is already profitable and generates more than $200 million in annual revenue. It also gives Archer an entry into military drones and defense, while Wisk brings autonomous eVTOL technology and SkyGrid adds an aviation software business.

That diversification changes the risk profile. Archer is no longer entirely dependent on waiting for its air taxi to receive certification before generating meaningful revenue. Its defense ambitions, drone operations and aviation software provide additional potential routes to monetization, although the Boeing transaction also introduces integration and execution risks.

Valuation further favors Archer in AA’s view. Joby’s market cap of roughly $6.25 billion compares with around $119.5 million of estimated 2026 revenue, or about 52 times visible revenue. Archer’s post-deal market cap would be approximately $5.17 billion, while Insitu alone contributes more than $200 million of existing annual revenue. That works out to roughly 26 times visible revenue.

Neither stock is cheap based on current revenue, and both still depend heavily on future growth. Archer therefore remains a speculative investment. Still, AA believes its combination of air taxis, defense, drones, software and existing revenue provides a broader path forward than Joby’s more certification-dependent story.

For AA, the conclusion is to close the Joby-Archer pair trade, have a speculative Buy on Archer and keep Joby at Hold (i.e., Neutral) until there is greater visibility on certification. Archer still faces deal-closing, integration and cash-burn risks, while Joby retains its certification advantage. The big difference is that Archer now has more than one route to generating value while the industry waits for eVTOL certification. (To watch AA’s track record, click here)

The Street takes a similar stance. JOBY gets a Hold consensus rating, although, somewhat paradoxically, its $11.50 average price target offers 12-month upside of 87%. ACHR is rated a Strong Buy, its $11.60 average target pointing to one-year gains of 124%. (See JOBY stock forecast or ACHR stock forecast)

data.description:
Rocket Lab (NASDAQ:RKLB) is moving closer to becoming a much broader space company. Its planned acquisition of Iridium would add a major satellite network and new commercial opportunities to Rocket Lab’s existing launch and space-systems businesses, giving the company more control across the space value chain.

Just as importantly, one of the biggest financial concerns surrounding the deal has now been addressed. Rocket Lab has raised roughly $1.9 billion and issued about 29 million shares, allowing it to terminate the $3.6 billion bridge facility that had presented a significant financing risk.

Top investor Melissa Tucker believes Rocket Lab could benefit significantly from combining its existing operations with Iridium. The deal would give the company an established end market for some of its technology while opening doors in areas such as positioning, navigation and timing (PNT), the Internet of Things (IoT), aviation and maritime communications.

Tucker also sees an opportunity to use Rocket Lab’s existing capabilities to build and launch future Iridium satellites internally. That could reduce costs and give the company greater control as Iridium eventually needs to refresh its constellation.

Meanwhile, Rocket Lab’s core business continues to build momentum. Its backlog has reached $2.36 billion, while the company has introduced its GHOST containerized launch system, designed to give customers greater flexibility with Electron and Haste launches.

But with the big financing overhang now removed, attention can turn to the company’s growth prospects, with the biggest piece of the investment story being Neutron, Rocket Lab’s next-generation reusable medium-lift rocket, which is being developed to carry larger payloads into orbit than the company’s Electron rocket. Management has indicated that the rocket’s first launch could move into 2027, and Tucker sees a successful early launch as an important catalyst. She then expects Neutron to add roughly $950 million by that point if its launch cadence develops as planned. The financial picture will change after the acquisition. Rocket Lab had $2.3 billion in cash and just $134 million of debt at the end of 2Q26, but Tucker expects the combined company to have around $1.2 billion in cash and $1.9 billion in debt following the transaction. Iridium’s cash generation should nevertheless reduce some of the dilution concerns that existed previously.

The main risks are execution-related. A significant Neutron delay would affect the company’s longer-term growth assumptions, while Electron needs sufficient demand to maintain its expansion. Tucker also sees Iridium integration and the ability to develop new markets as important factors, alongside the possibility of further share issuance if Rocket Lab needs additional capital.

However, those risks do not outweigh the positives. As such, the 5-star investor rates RKLB stock a Buy.  (To watch Tucker’s track record, click here)

data.title: Micron Earnings Are About to Hit – Is a Stock Split Coming? Top Investor Weighs In
data.description:
It’s a big day for the AI trade, and for memory stocks in particular.Most of all, it’s a hugely important day for Micron (NASDAQ: MU) investors. The memory giant faces a major test as it is due to report its latest earnings after the market closes. The results will be closely watched because Micron has become one of the clearest beneficiaries of the AI boom, with soaring demand for memory helping drive both its sales and profits to unprecedented levels.

The company is one of the world’s three prominent memory-chip manufacturers, alongside Samsung and SK Hynix. A supply shortage has sent memory prices surging, creating an unusually profitable environment for Micron. Its June quarter highlighted just how dramatic the turnaround has been, with revenue reaching $41.5 billion (up 346% vs. the same period last year) and net income climbing from $1.89 billion to $28.2 billion.

Wall Street expects another huge quarter. Analysts are looking for fourth-quarter revenue of around $51.4 billion, up roughly 354% year over year, while adjusted earnings per share are expected to rise from $3.03 to $31.71. If those estimates are met, Micron would be trading at less than 9 times run-rate earnings, while its forward P/E based on expected fiscal 2027 earnings would be below 7.

Promotion

Explore why XOVR invested in Kalshi and how it identifies innovative private companies before they reach the public markets.

Top investor Jeremy Bowman, who contributes to The Motley Fool and ranks among the top 1% of investors on TipRanks, thinks that leads to an interesting question: what could Micron do next to return more capital to shareholders?

With Micron’s shares now above the $1,000 mark, Bowman believes a stock split deserves serious consideration. Micron has not split its shares since 2000, but its enormous rally has put it among the highest-priced stocks in the S&P 500. Nvidia faced a similar situation before carrying out a 10-for-1 split in 2024, when its shares were trading at roughly $1,200.

A split would not alter Micron’s underlying value or financial performance. Instead, it would divide the existing shares into a larger number of lower-priced shares. Bowman argues that this could make the stock more accessible to individual investors and employees, while potentially making options trading more practical and improving liquidity.

There is also a signaling element. A stock split can indicate that management believes a company’s share price has room to keep climbing. Research from Bank of America has also found that companies have historically tended to perform well in the year following a split, although the timing of these moves can itself reflect management’s confidence in future performance.

Micron has already delivered enormous gains, with its shares up more than 1,000% over roughly the past year and a half. That leaves investors looking for the company to raise its capital returns. Micron is currently restricted in how much it can spend on share buybacks under the CHIPS Act, but those restrictions are set to expire on December 9. That could give the company greater flexibility to accelerate repurchases as its profits and cash generation soar.

A higher dividend is another possibility, particularly with Micron’s yield having fallen to just 0.05% following the huge rise in its share price. Nvidia recently took a similar step by raising its dividend substantially while also announcing a major new share-buyback authorization.

For Bowman, however, the combination of a four-figure share price and exceptional earnings growth makes a stock split a particularly logical next step. “Doing so would reward investors, reset the stock price, and make it more accessible,” the 5-star investor summed up. “There’s a good chance Micron splits its stock before the end of the year, and the stock could soar if it does.” (To watch Bowman’s track record, click here)

We’ll soon find out whether that actually happens, but in any case, Wall Street maintains a bullish stance ahead of the print. The stock has a Strong Buy consensus rating, based on 20 Buys vs. 1 Hold. Going by the $1,469.25 average price target, shares will be changing hands for a 37% premium a year from now. data.title: ‘Let It Print,’ Says Investor About Sandisk Stock
data.description:
Sandisk (NASDAQ:SNDK) has been enjoying the fruits of a major shift in the memory market. AI data-center expansion has been driving massive demand for NAND flash and enterprise SSDs. That demand has tightened supply and given Sandisk much greater pricing power than it has historically enjoyed. The result has been a significant improvement in the company’s profitability, but it has also left investors debating how sustainable the current boom can be.

The main question now is whether that demand can continue supporting Sandisk’s extraordinary profit profile. The memory industry is notoriously cyclical, so investors cannot ignore the possibility of an eventual downturn. For now, however, an investor using the pseudonym Quad 7 Capital (Q7) believes there are few signs that AI-related storage demand is weakening, and sees the fundamental case for Sandisk as intact.

One of Q7’s biggest arguments is that AI spending continues to support the memory market. Hyperscalers and enterprise tech companies are still spending aggressively on data-center infrastructure, and Q7 argues that this type of spending is relatively insulated from traditional macroeconomic pressures. Companies now view AI infrastructure as strategically important, meaning higher interest rates, inflation and energy costs have not yet translated into weaker demand for high-performance storage.

Promotion

High conviction on SNDK? Try Tradr's SNXX or SNDQ

Sandisk’s addition to the S&P 100 is another positive development. The move should result in additional buying from funds that track the index, while also highlighting the company’s growing importance within the technology sector.

Meanwhile, the upcoming fiscal Q1 2027 results (Oct. 29) will provide an important test of the thesis. Sandisk has guided for revenue of $10.3 billion to $10.8 billion and adjusted EPS of $44 to $46. The current consensus is around $10.55 billion in revenue and $46.18 in EPS. Gross margins are expected to reach an unusually high 83% to 85%, reflecting the favorable pricing environment created by the memory shortage. Q7 believes the company could exceed those expectations if current demand trends continue.

The investor also argues that the valuation deserves attention. Although the stock has risen dramatically, earnings have grown so rapidly that the forward multiple remains relatively low. Based on projected fiscal 2027 earnings, Sandisk is trading at a single-digit forward P/E. The recently authorized $14 billion buyback could provide another source of support while reducing the share count.

That said, there are still meaningful risks to consider. Sandisk remains heavily exposed to NAND memory and enterprise storage, leaving it vulnerable to the industry’s traditional boom-and-bust cycle. A sudden increase in supply could weaken pricing and compress today’s exceptionally high margins. A slowdown in AI infrastructure spending could have a similar effect. Execution also matters, while the elevated expectations surrounding the next earnings report mean even a strong result could disappoint investors if it falls short of what the market has already priced in.

However, those don’t overwhelm the bull case. “Yes, the cyclical risks of the memory market are ever-present, but the momentum of AI infrastructure spending is a rising tide lifting this boat higher than anyone anticipated,” Q7 summed up. “Buy the stock, let the AI data center buildout run its course, and enjoy the ride.”

Accordingly, Q7 rates SNDK stock a Buy. (To watch Quad 7 Capital’s track record, click here)

Most of the Street’s analysts are thinking along the same lines. With a mix of 15 Buys and 2 Sells, SNDK receives a Strong Buy consensus rating. At $2,195.29, the average price target implies shares will climb by 26% in the months ahead. (See SNDK stock forecast)

data.title: ‘This Could Be Major for Rocket Lab Stock,’ Says Investor
data.description:
Rocket Lab (NASDAQ:RKLB) is moving closer to completing its roughly $8 billion acquisition of Iridium, after Iridium shareholders overwhelmingly approved the deal. The transaction, announced in July, would combine Rocket Lab’s launch and spacecraft businesses with Iridium’s global satellite communications network.

The deal values Iridium at $54 per share, with $27 paid in cash and the remainder delivered in Rocket Lab stock. Assuming regulatory approval, the companies expect the transaction to close around the middle of next year.

Taking the measure of the deal, investor Eric Volkman, who contributes to The Motley Fool, believes it could give Rocket Lab a valuable new asset while creating a more vertically integrated space business. Iridium brings an established satellite network, spectrum rights and decades of experience in global communications, complementing Rocket Lab’s existing launch and spacecraft operations.

Iridium’s satellite constellation also gives it a distinctive position in the market. Its low-Earth-orbit satellites operate across multiple orbital planes, allowing the company to provide coverage across the entire planet, including remote locations. That is a significant advantage in areas where conventional communications infrastructure is limited.

The company does face competition from SpaceX’s Starlink, which has been expanding its satellite connectivity capabilities. Starlink has the advantage when it comes to speed and latency, making it better suited to applications such as internet browsing and video streaming. Iridium’s network is designed more for lower-bandwidth uses, including voice and other specialized communications.

Volkman nevertheless sees the Rocket Lab-Iridium combination as something different from SpaceX’s much broader collection of businesses. Rocket Lab would be bringing together operations that have an obvious connection: launching rockets, building spacecraft and operating satellite communications infrastructure. That could allow the combined company to capture more of the value generated across the space technology chain.

The financial profile of Iridium is another important part of the equation. Unlike many companies operating in the space sector, Iridium is already profitable and generates meaningful free cash flow. It produced nearly $300 million in free cash flow last year, giving Rocket Lab a business that can contribute cash rather than simply requiring continued investment.

Rocket Lab has also said it has secured commitments covering the cash portion of the acquisition. With Iridium shareholders having now approved the transaction, Volkman sees the company moving closer to completing a deal that could materially expand Rocket Lab’s capabilities and give it a profitable communications operation alongside its existing space businesses. “Rocket Lab investors should be very pleased that this important deal is gaining serious altitude,” Volkman summed up. data.title: Is AMD Stock’s Latest Acquisition a Game-Changer? Top Analysts Offer Differing Verdicts
data.description:
AMD (NASDAQ:AMD) is making another major move to strengthen its position in the AI race with Nvidia. Following the market close yesterday (Monday), the chipmaker announced a definitive agreement to acquire AI model and research company World Labs for approximately $8.2 billion in an all-stock deal. The transaction would rank as AMD’s second-largest acquisition behind its purchase of Xilinx. It is expected to close by the end of 2026, pending regulatory approval and other customary closing conditions.

Based in San Francisco, World Labs specializes in spatial-intelligence models capable of generating, reconstructing, and simulating interactive 3D environments using text, images, and video. Its technology also extends to robotic learning and simulation.

The acquisition comes shortly after Nvidia moved further into the model layer with its acquisition of Hugging Face earlier in the month. For AMD, bringing World Labs in-house adds a model layer that could give the company greater visibility into the development of frontier AI workloads, potentially informing the direction of its CPU and GPU roadmaps.

The deal also adds another dimension to AMD’s ambitions in physical AI, a market the company expects could reach $200 billion by 2035. World Labs’ modeling and simulation capabilities complement AMD’s expanding portfolio of edge silicon while giving it additional AI software and modeling expertise. The company will also gain experienced AI researchers, including World Labs founder Fei-Fei Li, who will join AMD.

Last November, World Labs introduced its first commercial world model, Marble. The technology can turn text, images, panoramas, and video into dynamic 3D environments that can be edited and manipulated. World Labs made Marble available to developers through the World API in January. The model was subsequently incorporated into simulation workflows, including Nvidia’s Isaac Sim, an open-source, Omniverse-based framework designed to generate synthetic training data.

For embodied AI systems, access to sufficiently diverse environments remains a major challenge. Synthetic data generated on demand can help reduce the reliance on physical data collection, which can otherwise be time-consuming, costly, and limited in scope.

AMD expects World Labs’ expertise in models to provide a better understanding of how AI workloads are developing and, in turn, help shape its hardware, software, and broader systems strategy. The company says the acquisition supports its goal of building AI infrastructure around an open ecosystem.

The technology could also slot into AMD’s existing robotics portfolio. World Labs’ models and simulation capabilities would give the Kria AI SOM and Robotics Developer Platform, introduced at Advancing AI in July, a native model layer to complement AMD’s robotics-focused silicon. That includes the Ryzen AI Embedded X100, which combines Zen 5 CPU cores with RDNA 3.5 graphics.

So, how are analysts on Wall Street viewing the move?

Rosenblatt’s Kevin Cassidy, who ranks among the top 1% of Street stock experts, sees clear potential in the acquisition. “We view AMD’s acquisition of World Labs as expanding AMD’s AI software, modeling, simulation capabilities,” the 5-star analyst said. “The rapid AI market development is requiring system level knowledge well outside traditional semiconductor expertise. World Labs engineers can accelerate system level AI platform development while opening new markets such as robotics. We view the $8.2B all-stock transaction as a pull-in of necessary future R&D expense to develop this technology in-house. We are impressed with management’s aggressive decision making in expanding its AI prowess.”

Accordingly, Cassidy maintained a Buy rating on the shares, backed by a $700 price target, suggesting the shares will gain 14% over the coming months.  (To watch Cassidy’s track record, click here)

William Blair’s Sebastian Naji, another 5-star analyst, similarly sees the acquisition helping AMD “narrow the gap with Nvidia’s own model and simulation portfolio.”

Still, AMD’s strong performance this year makes Naji more cautious about the shares. The stock is up 184% year-to-date, and the analyst points to its elevated valuation. “At these levels, AMD trades at a price-to-earnings multiple of 39 times on our calendar 2027 estimate,” Naji, who ranks among the top 2% of Street stock experts, said. “While we believe that AMD should be a beneficiary of growing AI spend across GPUs and CPUs over the coming years, with intensifying competition in the data center and a valuation that leaves little room for error, we see a relatively balanced risk/reward equation for shares.”

To this end, Naji rates AMD as Market Perform (i.e., Neutral) without having a fixed price target in mind. (To watch Naji’s track record, click here)

Elsewhere on the Street, 5 other analysts also remain on the sidelines, yet with an additional 30 Buys, the stock claims a Strong Buy consensus rating. The average target clocks in at $648.07, implying shares will gain 6% over the coming months. (See AMD stock forecast)
